description: Four key concepts — what each means in care contexts, and how they support individuals to thrive and feel valued.
hero_image_caption: A support worker discussing care options with a service user at a day centre.
content_html:
Four Concepts That Underpin Quality Care

When individuals use health and social care services, they need more than physical support — they need to feel that they have a voice, that they belong, and that they can cope with life’s difficulties. Four interconnected concepts underpin this: active participation, inclusion, resilience, and self-concept. Understanding each one — and how they differ — is essential for any learner in health and social care.

Active Participation

Active participation is about ensuring that individuals have a genuine say in how they live their lives and how their care is delivered. It is not enough for a practitioner to simply ask “is that alright?” — active participation means creating the conditions in which a person can meaningfully contribute to decisions about their own support.

Consider a resident at Ferndale Care Home, 81-year-old Mr Osei, who has mild cognitive impairment. Active participation means his key worker sits with him each week to discuss which activities he would like to join, what time he prefers his personal care, and whether he wants family visits on the weekend. His preferences are recorded in his care plan and staff follow them. Mr Osei is not a passive recipient of care — he is an active participant in shaping it.

Key Fact

Active participation is about the individual having a say in their own care and life decisions. It is distinct from inclusion, which is about equal access for all. Both are essential in person-centred care but they address different things.

Inclusion

Inclusion goes beyond treating people fairly — it means actively ensuring that every individual can access services, opportunities and community life on an equal basis, regardless of their disability, culture, language, age, or any other characteristic. Inclusion is about removing barriers rather than simply tolerating difference.

At Riverside Mental Health Support Service, a young woman named Priya, 22, has a severe social anxiety disorder. If staff only offer group therapy sessions, Priya is effectively excluded from support. An inclusive service would offer one-to-one appointments, video consultations, or written communication options so that Priya can access the same quality of care as other service users. Inclusion means no one is shut out.

It is a common misconception that active participation and inclusion are the same thing. They are related but distinct: active participation is about having a say; inclusion is about having equal access. An exam question that asks students to explain both concepts must treat them as separate ideas with separate explanations.

Barriers to inclusion can be physical (a GP surgery without wheelchair access), communicative (no British Sign Language interpreter available), attitudinal (staff making assumptions based on a person’s age or ethnicity), or systemic (referral pathways that exclude those without a fixed address). Care providers are legally required under the Equality Act 2010 to make reasonable adjustments to ensure equal access. From a health and social care perspective, inclusion is also an ethical obligation — individuals who are excluded from services experience worse health outcomes, greater isolation, and lower levels of well-being.

Resilience

The specification defines resilience precisely: it is an individual’s ability to successfully adapt to life’s unexpected challenges, whether in the face of social disadvantage or other adverse conditions such as family or relationship problems, workplace worries, or financial difficulties. This definition is important because resilience is not simply “being tough” or “coping” — it is about adaptation, and the specification names the types of adversity that resilience must contend with.

Resilience is relevant in care settings because individuals often arrive having experienced significant adversity. A young person leaving foster care at 18, a patient newly diagnosed with a chronic condition, or an older adult who has recently been bereaved may all need support to build their capacity to adapt. Practitioners who understand resilience can work with individuals to develop strategies — rather than simply providing services that individuals remain dependent on.

Key Fact

Resilience is defined as an individual’s ability to successfully adapt to life’s unexpected challenges, either in the face of social disadvantage or other adverse conditions including family or relationship problems, workplace and financial worries. The word adapt — not just “cope” — is the key term.

Self-Concept

Self-concept describes how an individual thinks about, evaluates and perceives themselves. It includes both self-esteem (how much a person values themselves) and self-worth (their overall sense of who they are and what they are capable of). A positive self-concept is closely linked to a high level of emotional well-being.

Self-concept is not fixed — it changes across the lifespan and is shaped by experiences, relationships, and social contexts. A child who is consistently praised for their efforts develops a more positive self-concept than one who is frequently criticised. An adult who loses their job may experience a temporary dip in self-concept if their sense of identity was closely tied to their career. Understanding self-concept helps care practitioners support individuals whose experiences have led to a negative view of themselves.

These four concepts reinforce one another. When an individual is included in their community, they feel valued — this supports a positive self-concept. When they actively participate in decisions about their care, they develop a sense of control and agency — which builds resilience. An individual with a strong self-concept is better placed to adapt to adversity, because they believe in their own capacity to manage difficulties. Conversely, exclusion from services damages self-concept, lowers resilience, and reduces the individual’s ability to participate meaningfully in their own care. A practitioner who understands these links does not treat the four concepts as a checklist — they see them as a connected framework for promoting well-being.
exam_tip_html: A frequent error on questions about these four concepts is treating active participation and inclusion as the same idea. The command word ‘Explain’ requires you to give reasons for the difference, not just name two things. Write: active participation is about the individual having a say in their care (because this promotes their sense of agency and control); inclusion is about equal access for all (because it removes barriers that prevent individuals from using services). Use “because” and “therefore” to show the reasoning — that is what earns the third and fourth marks on a short explanation question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Active participation means individuals have a genuine say in their own care; inclusion means equal access for all regardless of need or background — they are related but distinct concepts.
  • Resilience is the ability to successfully adapt to life’s unexpected challenges, including social disadvantage and family, workplace or financial adversity.
  • Self-concept is how an individual thinks about and evaluates themselves; a positive self-concept supports high levels of emotional well-being and is shaped throughout life by experiences and relationships.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'active participation' in health and social care?
A) Ensuring every individual can access services on an equal basis
B) An individual's ability to adapt to unexpected challenges
C) Involving individuals in decisions about their own care and lives
D) How a person thinks about and evaluates themselves
practice_questions.marks: C) Involving individuals in decisions about their own care and lives [1 mark]. A describes inclusion; B describes resilience; D describes self-concept.

practice_questions.text: Identify two characteristics of inclusion in a health and social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct, accurate characteristics (max 2). Acceptable answers include: equal access for all individuals regardless of need [1]; removing physical, communicative or attitudinal barriers [1]; ensuring no individual is shut out of services [1]; reasonable adjustments made for different needs [1]. Two near-identical points (e.g. 'equal access' and 'fair access') score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'resilience' in a health and social care context.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the core meaning (ability to adapt to life's unexpected challenges); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' or 'therefore' (e.g. because it allows individuals to manage social disadvantage, family or workplace difficulties); 1 mark for a developed application or example (e.g. therefore a care worker can support a service user to build coping strategies rather than creating long-term dependence on services).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a practitioner at a day centre for adults with physical disabilities could promote active participation for the individuals they support.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for describing active participation accurately (individuals having a say in decisions about their care and daily activities) with reference to the day centre setting. 2 marks for a specific, plausible example with detail — e.g. holding a weekly group where service users vote on activities [1], then using individual key-worker meetings to record each person's personal preferences and reviewing these monthly [1]. Answers that describe inclusion instead of active participation are awarded a maximum of 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how self-concept is linked to resilience for individuals who use health and social care services.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies the link between self-concept (how individuals think about and value themselves) and resilience (adapting to adversity) with developed reasoning from at least two angles. Example content: a positive self-concept supports resilience because an individual who believes in their own capabilities is better placed to adapt when challenges arise; conversely, a negative self-concept (e.g. low self-esteem resulting from abuse or exclusion) can undermine resilience by making the individual feel unable to cope. May also explore the role of practitioner support in building both simultaneously. Uses 'because', 'therefore', 'this means that'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies the link with some development; may address only one direction of the relationship.

Developing (2 marks): Names both concepts but offers limited explanation of the connection.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one concept correctly with little or no link to the other.

practice_questions.text:
Fatima is 15 years old and lives in a residential children's home. She has experienced significant family disruption and has low self-esteem. She rarely joins in group activities and says she does not want to be involved in any decisions about her care.

Analyse how the key worker at the home could use active participation, inclusion and an understanding of resilience to support Fatima's well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Chains the analysis across all three concepts with reference to Fatima's specific circumstances. Example content: Active participation — the key worker could begin with small, low-pressure choices (e.g. what to eat for breakfast) rather than large care-plan decisions, because Fatima's low self-esteem means being asked to make major decisions immediately could feel overwhelming, therefore gradually building her sense of agency. Inclusion — offering one-to-one alternatives to group activities means Fatima is not excluded simply because of her preference, because inclusion requires removing barriers not insisting on conformity. Resilience — by praising small achievements and reflecting on past difficulties Fatima has managed, the key worker helps her recognise her own capacity to adapt, because resilience is built through experience of overcoming adversity with support. Candidate shows how the three concepts interact: active participation builds agency, agency supports resilience, inclusion ensures Fatima feels valued and her self-concept improves.

Secure (5–6 marks): Addresses all three concepts with mostly developed reasoning; some reference to Fatima's circumstances.

Developing (3–4 marks): Addresses two concepts with some development; links to Fatima's circumstances are partial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names concepts with little development or application.

knowledge_checks.q: What does 'active participation' specifically mean in health and social care?
options: Ensuring equal access to services for all individuals
Individuals having a genuine say in decisions about their own care and lives
The ability to adapt to unexpected challenges
Treating all service users with dignity and respect

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the correct specification definition of resilience?
options: Being mentally tough and refusing to show weakness
The ability to successfully adapt to life's unexpected challenges
Developing a high level of self-esteem over time
Accessing equal opportunities regardless of background

knowledge_checks.q: Inclusion means ensuring every individual has _____ access to services, opportunities and community life regardless of their needs.
Self-concept describes how an individual thinks about, evaluates and _____ themselves.
Match each concept to its correct definition:
right: Having a genuine say in decisions about your own care
Equal access to services regardless of need or background
Successfully adapting to life's unexpected challenges

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'active participation' mean in health and social care?
flashcard_questions.a: Individuals having a genuine say in decisions about their own care and lives.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'inclusion' mean in a care setting?
flashcard_questions.a: Ensuring equal access to services and opportunities for all, regardless of need or background.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between active participation and inclusion?
flashcard_questions.a: Active participation is about having a say; inclusion is about having equal access.

flashcard_questions.q: Give the specification definition of resilience.
flashcard_questions.a: The ability to successfully adapt to life's unexpected challenges, including social disadvantage and family, workplace or financial adversity.

flashcard_questions.q: What does self-concept describe in a service user?
flashcard_questions.a: How they think about and perceive themselves overall.

flashcard_questions.q: What two components make up self-concept?
flashcard_questions.a: Self-esteem (sense of personal worth) and self-worth (sense of identity and capability).

flashcard_questions.q: Why is self-concept described as dynamic?
flashcard_questions.a: It changes across the lifespan as new experiences shape it.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two types of adversity that the resilience definition specifically mentions.
flashcard_questions.a: Family or relationship problems, and workplace or financial worries.

flashcard_questions.q: How does active participation support resilience?
flashcard_questions.a: It gives individuals a sense of control and agency, which builds their capacity to adapt to challenges.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a barrier to inclusion in a care setting.
flashcard_questions.a: A GP surgery without wheelchair access, or no sign-language interpreter available.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is resilience about adapting rather than just coping?
flashcard_questions.a: Adaptation means changing how you manage challenges, not simply enduring them.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a positive self-concept support resilience?
flashcard_questions.a: An individual who values themselves believes in their capacity to manage difficulties.

glossary_terms.definition: An approach to care in which individuals are actively involved in decisions about their own lives and care, having a genuine say in what happens to them.
Ensuring that every individual has equal access to opportunities, services and community life, regardless of their needs, background or characteristics.

An individual's ability to successfully adapt to life's unexpected challenges, whether in the face of social disadvantage or adverse conditions such as family, relationship, workplace or financial worries.
How an individual thinks about, evaluates and perceives themselves, encompassing self-esteem, self-worth and how they relate to the world around them.
An individual's evaluation of their own worth as a person — the degree to which they value, accept and respect themselves.
A person's overall sense of their own capabilities, characteristics, identity and place in the world.

items.title: The Power of Vulnerability | Brené Brown | TED
items.description: Brown's celebrated talk on shame, belonging and self-worth — directly relevant to why self-concept matters in care settings.

items.title: The Skill of Self Confidence | Dr Ivan Joseph | TEDxRyersonU
items.description: A sport psychologist explains how self-confidence (a core component of positive self-concept) is built through deliberate practice.

items.title: Every Kid Needs a Champion | Rita Pierson | TED
items.description: A teacher's argument for human connection in care and education — illustrates how positive relationships support self-concept and inclusion.

items.title: The Pursuit of Happyness (2006)
items.description: Based on a true story — Chris Gardner's resilience in the face of homelessness and adversity is a compelling real-world illustration of adapting to life's unexpected challenges.

items.title: Mind — What Is Self-Esteem?
items.description: Mind's accessible guide to self-esteem and self-worth, written for a general audience — useful background reading on the psychological side of self-concept.

items.title: Young Minds — Building Resilience
items.description: Young Minds' practical resource on resilience strategies for young people — complements the specification definition with real support examples.

items.title: NHS — What Is Inclusion? (NHS England)
items.description: NHS England's plain-language overview of inclusion and equality in health and social care settings.
